A little about me

Curiosity first. Then a solution that fits.

I’m Khaleel, a Data Engineer who enjoys getting close to a problem before deciding how to build around it.

I began by helping collect and check university data. That work grew into scraping and automation workflows, where each source had its own structure and exceptions.

I’m already a Data Engineer by role. Now I’m deepening my skills toward broader, larger-scale data engineering, while building on the practical experience I have in extraction, ETL, data quality, and automation.

repeatableWorkflows:
3,000+submissions processed
70+portal workflows configured
94%success rate
1,200+hours saved

Latest project snapshot; figures change as the platform is used. A manual submission could take about 30 minutes. Success rate is successful jobs as a share of completed jobs.

The problem

Every portal had its own rules.

Fields, page flows, uploads, verification, and conditional questions changed from one site to another. A separate bot for every portal would multiply maintenance.

Each submission meant someone re-entering CRM details into another external portal. The same information needed different formats, and the page itself could change depending on earlier answers.

The core design question was how to support new portal workflows without adding another portal-specific code path every time.

Describe the portal. Reuse the workflow.

I designed the JSON configuration model and workflow editor so each portal’s steps and conditions could live in configuration. The shared workflow could interpret that description, while config changes could be made without redeploying the code.

Design choices

What I built, and why.

Prepare data before the run

A Python preparation step reshapes CRM names, dates, country codes, phone numbers, and yes/no values into portal-ready values. Missing fields are surfaced before the browser starts.

Let the page determine the branch

Configuration rules check what is actually present on the page, follow relevant answers, and skip questions that do not apply. This lets one workflow cover multiple form paths.

Design for human checkpoints

My manager proposed human involvement for verification steps. I implemented the handoff so a person can complete an OTP or CAPTCHA and the workflow can continue afterward.

Make run status clear

Retries handle temporary slow-page conditions, while clear run-status categories guide the next step for configuration, portal, connection, and human-checkpoint events.

My contribution

Configuration and decision layer

  • Designed the JSON configuration model and workflow editor.
  • Built data preparation and conditional form logic.
  • Implemented human handoffs, retries, and clear run-status routing.
  • Contributed updates to browser automation after its initial implementation.

Team contribution

Clear ownership boundaries

A teammate built the Chrome extension and RabbitMQ component and initially implemented browser automation. My manager proposed the human-checkpoint approach and managed the work.

The outcome

A workflow that could grow through configuration.

More portal variation could be handled while keeping the shared codebase consistent. The project continues to run internally, so its metric snapshot changes over time.

universityDataCollection:
Projects/Professional work

Data extraction · Quality · CRM workflows

University Course and Intake Data Collection

University information lived across sites with different layouts and behaviors. I built and maintained scripts to collect it, then prepared files for quality checks before CRM import.

My role Script development and updatesCreated 37 university scriptsContributed to 72 universities
Source-specific collection

I matched each script to its university’s page structure, navigation, and content formats, then organized the collected records for review.

One script per university

University pages presented course and intake information in different structures, so the scripts followed each source’s own layout and navigation.

The scripts gathered course names, intakes, attendance details, duration, and other information used to keep the internal CRM current. The output went through a quality-control step before import.

Match each source page

The work involved browser navigation, page-specific selectors, pagination, dropdowns, dynamic pages, and data normalization. Different site behavior meant each script needed to match its own source.

My contribution

Script creation and maintenance

I created and maintained source-specific extraction scripts, then integrated them with shared normalization functions for intake dates, course level, campus, duration, and attendance type.

Technical context

TypeScript + Playwright

The scripts used TypeScript and Playwright with shared processing and storage components from the wider project.

Why the process mattered

Useful data needed a quality gate.

Preparing generated files for QC kept extraction separate from the final CRM update, so data could be checked before it reached operational records.

Education Partner Priority Dashboard

The challenge

People needed to identify which partners deserved attention without inspecting raw MongoDB records one by one.

The hackathon was an individual challenge: three people each built their own dashboard. I created mine independently, and it stood out to the CTO, who praised the design and shared it with other teams.

Make the record set easier to explore

The dashboard let staff search and filter partners by country, status, publish status, data source, recruitment type, and related attributes. Charts summarized the matching records, while a paginated table supported review of individual partners.

The prototype gave the CRM team a concrete reference for filtering and dashboard capabilities they later implemented directly in the CRM.

Public-data boundary: Portfolio illustrations use mock data; no live partner records or business results are shown.

How I approached it

Define the rules before the interface.

I specified the architecture and the business calculations, then used AI to generate much of the code and reviewed and refined the result.

Filter the same set everywhere

Charts always summarize the complete filtered set, independently of the current table page.

Use a weighted priority signal

A base score plus tag weights creates a consistent relative signal to support partner review.

Show several dimensions

Country, status, publish status, and recruitment types each add a different view. A partner with multiple recruitment types can contribute to more than one chart category.

Keep the build transparent

I designed the architecture and business rules, then reviewed and refined the AI-generated frontend and backend implementation. The page labels the work as a hackathon prototype.

Optional technical detail: score and filter behavior

Priority score: start at 1.0 and add matching tag weights: Express +0.5; Exclusivity +0.3; MarketingBudget +0.3; Priority +0.2; RussellGroup +0.2; AtRisk +0.1. The result is rounded to two decimal places. Tag matching ignores case; repeated tags count repeatedly. AtRisk increases this score in the current implementation.

Filtering: different filter fields combine with AND. Multiple data sources, recruitment types, or recruitment partners combine with OR within their field. Selected tags combine with AND, while charts summarize all matching records across table pages.

Architecture: HTML and vanilla JavaScript with Chart.js and Tailwind styling; Node.js, Express, and TypeScript APIs; MongoDB data normalized into an indexed in-memory store; Firebase sign-in and token verification; Jest and Supertest coverage configured.

Recognition and next step

A prototype that gave the team something concrete to build on.

The CTO’s response and the later CRM direction showed the value of making the idea tangible. The prototype gave the CRM team a clear reference for capabilities they later implemented in the CRM.

Codebase quality · AI workflows · Data updates

University Entry Requirement Monitoring

Entry requirements can be university-wide, nationality-specific, or course-specific. The workflow checks updates against existing records and routes the next action.

My role Maintenance and workflow supportPrimary implementation Colleague-ledAI use Ticket interpretation
Monitoring across levels

Requirements span university, nationality, and course levels, with updates gathered from related university emails.

Some entry requirements apply across a university. Others vary by nationality or by course. A monitoring workflow needs to find the relevant update and compare it with the current database record before an update is prepared.

Jira tickets are the checkpoint for updates. A scheduled bot checks tickets, follows the ticket to the related university email, and compares the email content with existing data. When requirements change, the workflow prepares an import file; matching records let the ticket close and the scheduled process continue.

My contribution was keeping the workflow dependable

A colleague led the primary implementation. I supported the system through codebase and script maintenance, quality checks, storage improvements, README documentation, updates from generated files, and Hermes-based checkpoint bots and schedules.

My work

Maintenance and quality

  • Maintained scripts and codebase quality.
  • Improved project READMEs and documentation.
  • Built configurable scheduled checkpoint bots in Hermes.
  • Updated records from generated files.

Team boundary

Colleague-led implementation

My colleague led the implementation; my contribution focused on dependable maintenance, scheduled checkpoints, documentation, and data updates.

A practical use of AI

Adapt the tool to the messy part of the process.

Ticket wording varies. AI helps interpret that checkpoint; explicit workflow rules handle schedules, comparisons, and ticket movement.
